title: Except nobody meant to spell it that way.
description:
Except nobody meant to spell it that way. The founders were reaching for 'googol', a mathematician's word for an enormous number. The company carries a typo of it, kept because the misspelling was the domain that happened to be free.

A googol is 1 followed by a hundred zeros. A nine-year-old, Milton Sirotta, coined the word in 1920; his uncle, the mathematician Edward Kasner, wrote it into a book. Google's founders were aiming for it.

A Stanford graduate student sharing Larry Page's office. Brainstorming names, he went to check whether 'googol' was a free domain, but typed 'google.com' by mistake. It was available. Page registered it the same day, 15 September 1997.

The number was named by a child. The company was named by a typo. Neither was the plan.

Sources:
- https://graphics.stanford.edu/~dk/google_name_origin.html (Stanford University, David Koller, January 2004; read in full 27 August 2026): established, from Koller's Stanford colleagues in the office where Google was born, that in 1996 Larry Page and Sergey Brin called their search engine 'BackRub'; that in September 1997, brainstorming a new name, Sean Anderson suggested 'googolplex' and Page shortened it to 'googol'; that Anderson, checking whether the domain was free, mistakenly searched for 'google.com', which was available; and that Page registered google.com that day, the registration record dating from 15 September 1997.
- https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/SH/kasner_sh.pdf (MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, 'Edward Kasner and how Google got its Name'; read in full 27 August 2026): established, quoting Kasner and Newman's 1940 book Mathematics and the Imagination, that 'googol' was coined in 1920 by Kasner's nine-year-old nephew Milton Sirotta as a name for 1 followed by a hundred zeros, and that a googolplex is a still larger number, 1 followed by zeros 'until you get tired'.
